notes.meaning: God asks Job whether he can catch the great water beast Leviathan on a hook or tie down its tongue with a rope. A fisherman can catch ordinary river fish, but no human can hook and reel in this massive beast. God uses this question to show Job that certain creatures are completely beyond human power.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars note that ancient Canaanite writings describe a similar multi-headed sea monster named Lotan.

notes.meaning: God asks if Job can put a rope through Leviathan's nose or run a hook through its jaw. Fishermen often ran cords through the gills or noses of small fish to carry them or keep them alive in the water. Leviathan is far too wild and mighty for anyone to handle or lead like a caught fish.

The Lord asks ironically whether Leviathan will plead for its life or speak gentle words to beg for mercy. A defeated human enemy might beg a conqueror to spare him, but this monster never surrenders. It knows no fear and will never humble itself before man.

God asks if the beast will make an agreement to become Job's lifelong servant. In ancient times, a servant could agree to stay in a household forever, but Leviathan cannot be tamed or put to work. It belongs to God's wild world and will never serve human masters.

The Lord asks whether Job could keep Leviathan as a pet like a little bird or put it on a leash for his young maidservants. People often caught small songbirds and tied strings to them for entertainment, but this beast is made to cause terror, not to provide amusement. It reminds man that creation does not simply exist for human diversion.

God asks if fishing partners can bargain over the creature or cut it up to sell among traders. Leviathan is so huge and dangerous that ordinary merchants cannot catch it or turn its body into goods to sell. Human commerce has no power over such a monster.

The Lord asks if Job can stick harpoons into Leviathan's hide or strike its head with fishing spears. Its thick skin and hard skull turn away the sharpest hunting tools. Ordinary human weapons simply cannot pierce it to bring it down.

God warns that anyone who tries to lay a hand on Leviathan will never forget the awful struggle and will never try it again. Merely touching the monster would bring swift danger and pain. This warning shows that stepping into a fight against superior power is total folly.

Any hope a hunter has of capturing or overpowering Leviathan is completely useless. A person would collapse in fear at the mere sight of it before even striking a blow. Looking upon the beast is enough to crush human confidence.

If no human is brave enough to wake or challenge Leviathan, God asks how anyone can dare to stand against Him. The creature is only one of God's works, yet it terrifies the boldest men. If man shrinks back from the creature, he cannot challenge the Creator who made it.

God declares that no one has ever given Him anything first that would put Him in their debt, because everything under heaven belongs to Him. Job cannot demand an explanation or claim that God treats him unfairly, since God owes nothing to any creature. Everything we have is a free gift from the Lord.

differ.view: This verse shows that people cannot earn God's favor or place Him in debt by their good deeds.

notes.meaning: God announces that He will speak openly about Leviathan's limbs, immense power, and well-formed body. Even though the beast is terrifying, its structure shows the wisdom and craftsmanship of the Creator. God invites Job to look closely at how skillfully this creature was formed.

The Lord asks who can peel back the creature's outer skin or approach its mouth with a bridle to steer it. Its tough outer hide acts like armor that cannot be stripped away. No person can control its jaws as if it were a common farm animal.

God asks who can force open the monster's mouth, which is ringed with terrifying rows of teeth. These sharp teeth are built to grip and tear anything in their path. The sight of its gaping jaws makes any human tremble in fear.

Leviathan's back is covered with rows of scales that fit together like locked shields sealed with wax. They are joined so tightly that not even air can pass between them. Because its natural armor holds fast and cannot be broken apart, weapons cannot harm it.

When Leviathan snorts or expels breath, the spray catches the sunlight and flashes like light. Its eyes shine brightly through the water, resembling the reddish glow of dawn. These vivid pictures capture how striking and awe-inspiring the beast appears when breaking the water's surface.

The beast's hot breath shoots out like burning torches, sparks, and clouds of thick smoke from a heated pot. Its breath seems powerful enough to set coals on fire with its fierce heat. God uses poetic imagery of fire and smoke to describe the overwhelming fury and heat of the monster's exhaled breath.

Immense strength makes its permanent home in the beast's powerful neck. Wherever it moves, panic and dismay leap ahead of it, leaving everyone terrified. The creature's mere arrival drains the courage from all who see it.

The folds of Leviathan's flesh are knit tightly together, remaining firm and solid rather than loose or flabby. Its chest and heart are as hard as stone, just like a heavy lower millstone that grinds grain. This description highlights both its rock-solid body and its utterly fearless spirit.

When Leviathan rears up from the water, even the strongest and bravest warriors are filled with dread. The crashing waves and violent thrashing it causes send hunters fleeing in confusion and fear for their lives. No human courage can stand firm against such an overwhelming sight.

Swords, spears, darts, and body armor are useless against this monster. It treats strong iron weapons as if they were dry straw and hard bronze as rotten wood. Human fighting tools lose all their power against its natural defenses.

Arrows shot from bows cannot drive Leviathan away, and heavy slingstones hit it like harmless bits of chaff. Wooden war clubs feel like light straw, and it laughs at the whistling sound of a thrown spear. The most dangerous weapons of ancient warfare fail to leave a scratch.

The underside of the beast has sharp, pointed scales like broken pieces of pottery. When it lies down and drags itself through the mud, it leaves deep grooves as if a heavy threshing sledge had rolled across the ground. Even its belly is armored and impervious to sharp rocks.

When Leviathan thrashes and swims, it churns the water until the deep boils and foams like a pot of spiced ointment. It leaves behind a glowing, frothy wake that makes the dark water look like the white hair of an old man. Its incredible power completely stirs up the waters around it.

Nothing on the face of the earth can match Leviathan in strength or ferocity. It was created completely devoid of fear, shrinking back from no other beast or human hunter. God created it to stand unthreatened in its watery world.

The beast looks down with disdain on all other large, proud creatures, reigning as king over all wild animals. By showcasing this unconquerable king of beasts, God shows that He alone holds ultimate power over every proud creature on earth. Job is reminded to bow in humble submission before such an awesome Creator.

other.label: Catholic and Orthodox
other.view: Several early Christian teachers interpreted Leviathan as a symbol of Satan, the ruler of all proud spirits.
